sī

conjunction: the indicative for a real condition, the present or perfect subjunctive for a supposed one, the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive for one contrary to fact · Wiktionary

Where English puts a present after “if” for the future, Latin says the future or the future perfect: sī mē rogābis, if you ask me; sī … adjēcerit deus, if God grants (Sen. Ep. 12.9). Contrary to fact: the imperfect for the present (sī … concēderet, possem), the pluperfect for the past (sī … nātus esset). Sī mē amās, the “please” of Cicero’s letters.

Other words

  • quod sī (quodsī) — but if, now if

    conjunction, with the moods of sī · also used · classical · Petr. 50.1: quod sī nōn frangerentur, māllem mihi quam aurum

    Takes up what has just been said: “and if, but if”.

Examples

  • sī vīs, potes

    if you want to, you canHor. S. 2.6.39

  • sī mē rogābis, sīc dīcam

    if you ask me, I shall say thisCato Agr. 1.7

  • crāstinum sī adjēcerit deus, laetī recipiāmus

    if God adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladlySen. Ep. 12.9

  • Bis est grātum quod opus est, ultrō sī offerās.

    What is needed is twice welcome if you offer it unasked.Publ. B 1

  • sī mihi Nausicaa patriōs concēderet hortōs, Alcinoō possem dīcere “mālō meōs”

    if Nausicaa offered me her father’s gardens, I could say to Alcinous: “I prefer my own”Mart. 12.31.9–10

  • sī in Parthiā nātus esset, arcum īnfāns statim tenderet

    had he been born in Parthia, he would have drawn a bow as a babySen. Ep. 36.7

  • sed cūrā, sī mē amās, ut valeās

    but please, take care of yourselfCic. Fam. 9.20.3

See also unless, if not, even if, whether.
